claims.claim: Malcom McLean co-founded McLean Trucking Co., based in Red Springs, North Carolina, and drove trucks himself.
claims.episode_span: Malcom McLean, a North Carolina trucker, looked at the physical reality of freight and asked what would remain if the handling steps themselves were removed rather than merely sped up.
claims.supporting_quote: The same year, McLean, his brother, Jim, and his sister, Clara, founded McLean Trucking Co. [ 2 ] Based in Red Springs, North Carolina , McLean Trucking started hauling empty tobacco barrels, with McLean as one of the drivers.

claims.claim: On April 26, 1956 the converted tanker SS Ideal-X sailed from Port Newark for Houston carrying 58 containers.
claims.episode_span: McLean’s company demonstrated the principle on the Ideal X in 1956 by loading fifty-eight boxes in a single day rather than the week that equivalent break-bulk tonnage would have required.
claims.supporting_quote: On April 26, 1956, with 100 invited dignitaries present, one of the converted tankers, the SS Ideal-X (informally dubbed the "SS Maxton" after McLean's hometown in North Carolina), was loaded and sailed from the Port Newark-Elizabeth Marine Terminal , New Jersey, for the Port of Houston , Texas, carrying 58 35-foot (11 m) Trailer Vans , [ 9 ] later termed containers, along with a regular load of liquid tank cargo.

claims.claim: Hand-loading a ship cost $5.86 a ton, versus 16 cents a ton with containers — a roughly 36-fold saving in loading cost.
claims.episode_span: Containerization reduced the cost of moving general cargo by roughly an order of magnitude once ports and fleets were reconfigured around the box, a figure established in economic histories of the period.
claims.supporting_quote: Hand-loading a ship cost $5.86 a ton at that time. Using containers, it cost only 16 cents a ton to load a ship, 36-fold savings. Containerization also greatly reduced the time to load and unload ships.

claims.claim: The container design incorporated twistlock fittings at each of the four corners so the box could be secured and lifted mechanically by cranes.
claims.episode_span: The first concrete move was to select a size and corner-casting geometry that allowed a single spreader to engage the box mechanically at any point in the journey, eliminating the need for longshoremen to enter the hold or open the container.
claims.supporting_quote: The design incorporated a twistlock mechanism atop each of the four corners, allowing the container to be easily secured and lifted using cranes.

claims.claim: Before containerization, crews of 20 to 22 longshoremen packed individual cargoes into a ship's hold by hand.
claims.episode_span: a single cargo ship might spend a week or more in port while hundreds of longshoremen carried crates, barrels, and bales one by one from truck to hold and back again
claims.supporting_quote: Prior to highly mechanized container transfers, crews of 20 to 22 longshoremen would pack individual cargoes into the hold of a ship. After containerization, large crews of longshoremen were not necessary at port facilities

claims.claim: The Ideal X left Port Newark on April 26, 1956 with 58 thirty-five-foot containers loaded in under eight hours, at a time when break-bulk cargo could take several days to load and ships sat in port while goods were handled one by one.
claims.episode_span: In the 1950s a single cargo ship might spend a week or more in port while hundreds of longshoremen carried crates, barrels, and bales one by one from truck to hold and back again.
claims.supporting_quote: The containers on board were 35 feet long, consistent with standard truck trailer sizes at the time, and were loaded onto the ship in less than eight hours. At a time when breakbulk cargo could take several days to load, that speed marked a major shift, as ships often remained in port for extended periods while goods were handled one by one, driving up costs and increasing the risk of delays and damage.

claims.claim: McLean calculated that in 1956 loading a medium-sized ship the conventional way cost $5.83 a ton, versus under $0.16 a ton with containers (Wikipedia's figure is $5.86; the ratio is the same, about 36x).
claims.episode_span: In the break-bulk era that finished handling cost could exceed the material floor by a factor large enough to make the Idiot Index of ocean freight startlingly high, because the same ton of cargo might be touched a dozen times between factory door and foreign warehouse.
claims.source_title: First Containership, Ideal-X, 1956 | The Geography of Transport Systems
claims.supporting_quote: McLean calculated that in 1956, loading a medium-sized ship the conventional way cost $5.83 a ton. By comparison, loading containers (using the Ideal-X as a frame of reference) would cost less than $0.16 per ton.

claims.claim: In break-bulk shipping port handling dominated the voyage: on the 1954 SS Warrior transatlantic run the sea crossing took ten and a half days while some cargo spent over three months in transit, and loading and unloading accounted for more than a third of the voyage's total cost.
claims.episode_span: The result was that ships spent long stretches of their lives tied up in port rather than at sea, capital sat idle in hulls tied to wharves, and the effective Idiot Index of freight movement remained high
claims.source_title: The Box That Shrank the World by Marc Levinson (Works That Work magazine)
claims.supporting_quote: Although the transatlantic voyage took only ten and a half days, some of the cargo spent more than three months in transit. Loading and unloading the ship accounted for more than one-third of the total cost of the voyage.

claims.claim: Container adoption took a decade of struggle and required negotiations on standards so that almost any container could travel on any truck, train or ship.
claims.episode_span: The first concrete move was to select a size and corner-casting geometry that allowed a single spreader to engage the box mechanically at any point in the journey
claims.supporting_quote: It required years of high-stakes bargaining with two of the titans of organized labor, Harry Bridges and Teddy Gleason, as well as delicate negotiations on standards that made it possible for almost any container to travel on any truck or train or ship.
